query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using a eutectic high‐entropy alloy (specifically an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 type EHEA) as an interlayer in HEA multilayers will enable a transition between diffusion‐mediated creep and dislocation‐mediated creep because its lamellar microstructure creates highly coherent interfaces that can both block dislocation motion at lower temperatures and become permeable to atomic diffusion at higher temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayers with sharp, coherent interfaces between layers of a ductile FCC phase and a strengthening BCC/B2 or related phase.
generation.intervention: Introducing a thin layer of eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) at the interface between standard HEA layers.
generation.conditions: A range of elevated temperatures where both diffusion processes (e.g., Nabarro–Herring or Coble creep) and dislocation-mediated creep can be active; mechanical testing under controlled creep conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent lamellar interface within the eutectic HEA, which maintains structural order at lower temperatures yet allows increased atomic mobility at higher temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the coherent interfaces impede dislocation glide and suppress dislocation climb, stabilizing the microstructure; as temperature increases, enhanced atomic diffusion at these interfaces allows a switch to diffusion-mediated creep. Thus, the interlayer acts as a transition material controlling the dominant creep mechanism depending on operating conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable shift in the creep rate with temperature, with lower creep rates (dominated by dislocation-mediated mechanisms) at lower temperatures and a transition to diffusion-dominated creep at higher temperatures. This transition is expected to be tunable by adjusting the thickness and coherency of the eutectic interlayer.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers without the eutectic interlayer, where interface coherency is less systematically controlled, resulting in a less predictable balance between diffusion and dislocation creep.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to multilayered high‐entropy alloy coatings where the microstructural length scales (e.g., layer thickness, lamellar spacing) and temperature range are such that both diffusion and dislocation mechanisms compete. It may not hold if the interfaces become incoherent due to processing or if extreme temperatures promote complete recovery or recrystallization.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature range over which the transition occurs and the quantitative impact of the lamellar coherency on the creep rate are uncertain, pending systematic experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA multilayer coatings: one with a deliberately introduced eutectic HEA lamellar interlayer (AlCoCrFeNi2.1) and one without. Subject both to a series of creep tests over a controlled temperature range (e.g., from moderate to high temperatures where both mechanisms might compete). Microstructural analysis (using TEM and SEM) should be conducted before and after creep to evaluate interface coherency and phase stability.
measurements: Creep rate (strain vs time) as a function of temperature and applied stress
Microstructural evolution and interface coherency via TEM
Activation energies for creep from Arrhenius plots
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA multilayers with the eutectic interlayer do not exhibit a distinct, tunable change in the dominant creep mechanism—specifically, if the creep rate, activation energy, and microstructural markers (e.g., differences in dislocation density versus diffusional void formation) are not significantly different from the baseline samples across the temperature range—then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
